name: Diverticular disease and diverticulitis
definition: Diverticular disease is a condition in which small pouches in the wall of the large intestine cause symptoms, and diverticulitis is when those pouches become inflamed or infected.
overview: Diverticula are small pouches that push outward through weak spots in the wall of the large intestine. Most people develop some as they get older, and few of them ever have symptoms. When the pouches cause symptoms, bleeding or inflammation, doctors use the term diverticular disease. Diverticulitis, in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe. Complications are uncommon but can include a blockage, an abscess or a hole in the bowel.
causes: Small pouches form and push outward through weak spots in the wall of the large intestine.
Experts are not sure what causes diverticular disease and diverticulitis.
Diverticulitis happens when the pouches become inflamed or infected.
riskFactors: A diet low in fibre and high in red meat
Medicines such as NSAIDs and steroids
Genes may make some people more likely to develop the disease
signs: In severe illness, signs of sepsis such as confusion or pale, blotchy skin
complications: An abscess in the colon caused by infection
A fistula, an abnormal connection that may need surgery
diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the person's history, a physical examination and tests. Tests may include a colonoscopy or a CT scan, and blood tests that look for inflammation are commonly used.
treatment: Symptoms of diverticular disease are usually eased with painkillers such as paracetamol, bulk-forming laxatives and antispasmodic medicines. Antibiotics are used when diverticulitis is caused by infection. People admitted to hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein. Surgery to remove part of the colon may be considered for complications such as a fistula or a blockage.
prevention: The NHS describes gradually adding fibre with plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight as helpful steps. It is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the condition.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy rectal bleeding, or signs of sepsis. NHS 111 or a GP the same day is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, worsening or lasting tummy pain, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.

references.title: NICE: Diverticular disease: diagnosis and management (NG147)

sections.heading: What is the difference between diverticulosis, diverticular disease and diverticulitis?
sections.body:
The word diverticula describes small pouches that form in the wall of the large intestine, which is also called the bowel. Having the pouches, known as diverticulosis, usually causes no discomfort, and most people with them never notice. Sometimes they are found by chance during tests done for another reason.

Doctors speak of diverticular disease when the pouches lead to symptoms, bleeding, inflammation or complications. Without inflammation, the disease can cause constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or bloating. Diverticulitis is the stage in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, as the NHS describes it.

NIDDK, a United States institute, says experts are not sure what causes these conditions. It lists factors that may play a part, including genes, and says researchers are still studying changes in gut bacteria and immune problems.

sections.heading: What does diverticulitis feel like?
sections.body:
Diverticulitis most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe. The NHS lists severe, constant tummy pain and a high temperature among the signs, alongside constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and blood in the stool.

Pain, bloating and bowel changes can also occur with diverticular disease that is not inflamed. Without inflammation being shown by tests, the diagnosis is not settled by symptoms alone.

Complications are uncommon, according to the NHS. They can include a blockage, an abscess or a hole in the bowel, and they sometimes need surgery. NIDDK also lists bleeding, and explains that an infection can form an abscess in the colon. Pain that is severe or constant, a high temperature, or blood in the stool are the features the NHS highlights when it advises getting medical help.

sections.heading: How do doctors diagnose diverticulitis?
sections.body:
Doctors start with the person's history and a physical examination. Tests such as a colonoscopy or a CT scan may then be used to diagnose diverticular disease or diverticulitis.

A NICE evidence review notes that the white blood cell count and C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation, are commonly used to help diagnose diverticulitis and its complications. A review of diagnosis says the aim is to show inflammation and then to place it at a diverticulum using ultrasound or CT. The NICE review reports good sensitivity for CT, which means it picks up most true cases.

In an acute illness, blood tests together with CT are described by one review as the gold standard.

sections.heading: How is diverticulitis treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on whether the problem is diverticular disease or diverticulitis and on how unwell the person is. For diverticular disease, the NHS lists painkillers such as paracetamol, bulk-forming laxatives and antispasmodic medicines. Antibiotics are used when diverticulitis is caused by infection.

NICE guideline NG147 sets out different routes. People who are unwell all over the body but do not need referral are offered antibiotics by mouth. For people who are systemically well and have no conditions that raise the risk of infection, the committee noted that watchful waiting is an option. Those admitted to hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein.

Surgery to remove part of the colon, called a colectomy, may be recommended for complications such as a fistula or a blockage. NICE recommends against offering antibiotics or an aminosalicylate medicine to prevent diverticulitis from coming back.

sections.heading: Can diet and lifestyle make a difference?
sections.body:
The NHS self-care advice includes adding fibre to the diet gradually while drinking plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight. It also says NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen and opioids such as codeine can cause stomach problems and raise the risk of a bowel perforation.

NIDDK lists a diet low in fibre and high in red meat, little physical activity, NSAIDs and steroids, obesity and smoking as factors that may raise the risk of diverticulitis or its complications. MedlinePlus suggests a high-fibre, low-red-meat diet and not smoking. However, it also states that it is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the problem.

NIDDK describes age as a major factor, so lifestyle is only part of the picture. The NHS says most people develop some pouches as they get older, and that few have symptoms. Researchers are also still studying the roles of changes in gut bacteria and of immune problems.

sections.heading: When should I get help for tummy pain or a high temperature?
sections.body:
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, or being unable to pass stool or wind. The same applies to heavy bleeding from the back passage and to signs of sepsis, such as confusion, pale or blotchy skin, or abnormal temperature or breathing.

NHS 111 or the GP the same day is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, tummy pain that is getting worse or not settling, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down. Fever, severe pain and bleeding can also point towards complications such as an abscess, a blockage or a hole in the bowel, which the NHS says sometimes need surgery. The routes named are 999 for emergencies, NHS 111 or the GP the same day for urgent symptoms, and a routine GP appointment otherwise.

faqs.q: Is diverticulitis the same as diverticulosis?
faqs.a: No. Diverticulosis means having the small pouches in the wall of the large intestine, which usually causes no symptoms. Diverticular disease is the term used when the pouches cause symptoms or problems. Diverticulitis is when the pouches become inflamed or infected.

NICE guideline NG147 offers antibiotics by mouth to people who are unwell all over the body but not referred to hospital. It notes that watchful waiting is an option for people who are systemically well with no conditions that raise infection risk. People in hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein. NICE sets these out as recommendations for the clinician to apply to the individual.

faqs.q: Which painkillers does the NHS mention for diverticular disease?
faqs.a: The NHS lists painkillers such as paracetamol among the treatments for diverticular disease symptoms. It says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, and opioids such as codeine, can cause stomach problems and raise the risk of a bowel perforation. A pharmacist or GP can advise on the right choice for an individual.

Experts are not sure what causes it, according to NIDDK. NIDDK lists a low-fibre, high-red-meat diet as a factor that may raise risk, and MedlinePlus suggests a high-fibre, low-red-meat diet. MedlinePlus also says it is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the condition.

It can be. The NHS advises calling 999 for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy rectal bleeding or signs of sepsis. For blood or mucus in the stool, worsening pain, a high temperature or repeated vomiting, it advises NHS 111 or a GP the same day.
